newsitem.title: UK: Dollar slips, U.S. rate rise talk suffers setback.
newsitem.headline: Dollar slips, U.S. rate rise talk suffers setback.

text.p: LONDON, July 4 (Reuter) The dollar retreated, slipping to its lowest levels in a week against the yen, after Thursday's June U.S. jobs report set back expectations of how soon the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates.
The report showed the American jobless rate rose to 5 percent in June from a near 24-year low of 4.8 percent in May and that the pace of job creation in the private sector slowed.
"The dollar is slipping primarily in the wake of the payrolls data," said Gerard Lyons, the chief economist at DKB.
Dollar/yen, which earlier fell as low as 113.24, was at 113.24/29 at 0730 GMT from 113.42/52 late Thursday in Europe.
Dollar/mark was at 1.7482/89 from 1.7510/15 late yesterday. Its slide against the mark was slowed by the German currency's slump towards its lowest levels this year against the yen.
The mark fell to 64.70 yen, a whisker away from the 1997 low of 64.66 set on June 11. It was last at 64.70/72 yen from 64.85/87 late yesterday.

Shimpei Nukaya, a Japanese Economic Planning Agency official, said Friday that no consideration is currently being given to raising interest rates there from record lows. The comments were overshadowed by mounting expectations the Fed will not raise its target fed funds rate from 5.5 percent either.

"The upside risk for growth is in Japan, not the U.S., and given that the Fed may not have to raise rates in the second half of this year, it looks like dollar/yen will be in a bit of trouble," said Ian Morris, international economist at HSBC Markets.
The U.S. currency is also expected by analysts to pull back from the 40-month high of 1.7566 marks it reached Thursday before the release of the U.S. jobs data.
Still, these losses will be limited by traders' perception that German growth remains sluggish and concern that the planned European currency will be softer than the mark, they said.
"The only thing that will help the mark right now is the complete collapse of EMU," said Lyons at DKB. "Given that this looks very unlikely, mark/yen is a one-way bet and will go to 60 this year."
Mark weakness has been most pronounced against sterling, where concern about EMU and expectations that UK interest rates are poised to ratchet higher have been combined to potent effect.
Sterling has gained as much as 2.7 percent against the mark in the past three trading days, vaulting above 2.96 marks for the first time in almost six years on Thursday.
Its rise has gathered pace since the UK budget presentation Wednesday, which was seen by traders as leaving interest rate policy with most of the burden of curbing domestic demand.
Sterling/mark was last at 2.9490/00 from 2.9580/90 late Thursday in Europe.
Currency rading is expected by traders to become more subdued later in Europe because of the U.S. Independence Day holiday.
